g.text: Windows in SQL — TUMBLE, HOP, SESSION, and the watermark
TUMBLE 4 rows totalling 45 · HOP 7 rows totalling 78 · SESSION 5 rows, count unpredictable
4 rows, and the sums total 45 — the whole dataset
Every row of the input is in exactly one output row, so the totals reconcile against a batch job over the same data.
This is the SQL spelling of ch04's fixed window — same semantics, different syntax, nothing added.
Step 1/4 — TUMBLE — equal, non-overlapping, one row each
TUMBLE is the default to reach for and the easy one to reason about: 4 output rows, each input row counted once, totals summing to 45. If a
question names a period, this is the window, and the result reconciles against a batch run.
Windows in SQL — TUMBLE, HOP, SESSION, and the watermark
TUMBLE 4 rows totalling 45 · HOP 7 rows totalling 78 · SESSION 5 rows, count unpredictable
how many output rows each input row contributes to
7 output rows instead of 4, totalling 78 instead of 45 — because 6 input rows appear in 2 windows.
The output volume is size / slide = 120 / 60 = 2x. That is the intent, not a bug — and it means HOP totals must never be compared to the input.
Step 2/4 — HOP — overlapping, so a row appears several times
HOP answers "the rolling 120s figure, refreshed every 60s" and costs 2× the rows. The column to read is the third: 6 of 9 input rows land in 2
output rows, which is why the 78 total is correct and incomparable to the dataset's 45.
Windows in SQL — TUMBLE, HOP, SESSION, and the watermark
TUMBLE 4 rows totalling 45 · HOP 7 rows totalling 78 · SESSION 5 rows, count unpredictable
key "a" gets 3 rows and key "b" gets 2 — the row COUNT is data-dependent
TUMBLE and HOP have a row count you can compute from the time range. SESSION does not — it comes from how bursty the data was.
And the engine MERGES: a row arriving inside the gap between two existing sessions collapses them, which is a window boundary moving after the
Step 3/4 — SESSION — the engine merges windows as rows arrive
SESSION is the one window whose output row count cannot be predicted from the query: key "a" gets 3 rows and key "b" gets 2 over the same time
range. The merging in the note is what the engine is doing for you, and it is also why a SESSION result is always an updating stream.
Windows in SQL — TUMBLE, HOP, SESSION, and the watermark
TUMBLE 4 rows totalling 45 · HOP 7 rows totalling 78 · SESSION 5 rows, count unpredictable
WHEN A WINDOWED ROW IS EMITTED
the time attribute picks the bucket; the watermark picks the moment
never emitted — the watermark never passes its end
Without a watermark a windowed query over an unbounded stream could never emit anything, because "the window is done" would never become true.
1 of the 4 windows here is never emitted at all, and the SQL gives no hint of that.
Step 4/4 — and the watermark is what makes any of them correct
The query says which bucket a row goes in; the watermark says when the bucket speaks. Both are needed and only one is visible in the SQL — which
is why 1 window here is never emitted and nothing in the query text would tell you. The engine configures the watermark; you still chose the time
